title: "I do not absolve myself"
hookLine: cleared of all charges, Yusuf still says the self urges toward wrong unless Allah has mercy
last: THE FAT YEARS FEED THE THIN.

cards: Years in a cell, for something he didn't do. Then a messenger is at the door: the king wants you. The king has heard Yusuf's reading of the dream and says: bring him to me.
And Yusuf, still in the cell, tells the messenger: no. Go back to your master, and ask him about the women who cut their hands. He won't walk out under a cloud.
He wants the truth said out loud first.

teach.b: Surah Yusuf. The king calls in the women. They say: Allah preserve us, we know no evil of him.
And the Aziz's wife stands up and says it herself: now the truth is out. I tried to turn him from himself, and he is one of the truthful. Then comes a line commentators have argued over.
In Pickthall's translation: "I do not exculpate myself."
I don't clear myself. The self, the nafs, urges toward wrong, except the one my Lord has mercy on. Who says it?
Commentators such as al-Tabari say Yusuf: at the very moment he's declared innocent, he refuses to call himself pure.
Other scholars, including Ibn Kathir, read it as the Aziz's wife, still speaking, owning her part. The Arabic allows both. Our path follows the first; it's worth knowing the second.
Either way, nafs means the self, the soul, and it shares a root with nafas, breath. The Qur'an describes it at different stages. Here it's the nafs that urges toward wrong.
Elsewhere it's the self that blames itself when it slips. And near the end of the Qur'an, it's the self at peace, called back to its Lord, well-pleased.

teach.h: THE SELF THAT PUSHES, THEN RESTS.
teach.b: Muslim teachers, especially in the Sufi tradition, have seen a whole journey there: from the self that pushes, to the self that notices, to the self that rests.
Yusuf gives us the first honest step. Even innocent, even vindicated, he doesn't say, I'm fine. He says: I'm a self, and selves need mercy.
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ once said that if he'd been kept in prison as long as Yusuf, he'd have answered the summons at once. He was honoring Yusuf's patience.

how: Muslims speak of struggling with the nafs, the self, as a lifelong part of faith; Muslim teachers, Sufis especially, use the Qur'an's three descriptions (the self that urges wrong, the self that blames itself, the self at peace) to describe that journey.

o: a sin that a person has already confessed
the self, which pushes, notices, and can rest
the body, as opposed to the spirit within

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: Yusuf walked out of prison the moment the king called
he sent the messenger back: first ask about the women who cut their hands.
scholars agree who says "I do not absolve myself"
some, such as al-Tabari, say Yusuf; others, including Ibn Kathir, say the Aziz's wife.
the Qur'an describes the nafs at more than one stage
the self that urges wrong, the self that blames itself, and the self at peace.

games.q: you're Yusuf. after years in prison, the king's messenger says: the king wants you. you're free. what do you do?
o: go at once, before he changes his mind.
send him back: ask about the women who cut their hands.
ask for a reward for reading the dream.
games.why: he wouldn't leave under a cloud. the women cleared him, the Aziz's wife confessed, and only then came the line: I don't clear myself.

practice: Watch your mind for a minute like a busy street from a window: what it reaches for, a craving, a grudge, a little self-congratulation, a worry, and how often it wants to be right, seen, comfortable.
No fixing, no scolding, just seeing; near the end, say inside, as Yusuf did: I don't clear myself. If you pray, you can ask for mercy on the self you just watched.

wordCard.voice: Nafs. The self, the soul: the part of you that pushes, that can learn to notice, and can come to rest. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: self, soul; it shares a root with nafas, breath. Qur'an 12:53, the self that urges toward wrong.

carryVoice: Your line: I don't clear myself. Being proven right is a good moment to stay humble. See you on day sixty-seven.
